clues.kinetics: Absolute bioavailability is only about 4.7% at 100 mg, and food raises exposure by about 20%. It is 97.8% bound to plasma protein, and it leaves mainly in feces via bile.
clues.substance: Presented as an esylate salt; the active moiety has a molecular weight of 539.6.
clues.product: Approved under an NDA as 100 and 150 mg soft capsules, dosed twice daily.
clues.safety: No boxed warning and no contraindications. Bronchitis is the most frequent serious adverse reaction, and pneumonia the most common fatal one.
clues.indication: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, chronic fibrosing interstitial lung diseases with a progressive phenotype, and systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease.
clues.mechanism: Blocks several receptor tyrosine kinases, including PDGF, FGF and VEGF receptors, that are involved in fibrotic remodeling of lung tissue.

tell: A kinase inhibitor with an effective half-life of 9.5 hours and an absolute bioavailability of only 4.7%.

evidence.pk.tmaxH: Nintedanib reached maximum plasma concentrations approximately 2 to 4 hours after oral administration
evidence.pk.halfLifeH: The effective half-life of nintedanib in patients with IPF was 9.5 hours
evidence.pill: 150 mg: brown, opaque, oblong, soft capsules marked in dark gray
clues.kinetics: The absolute bioavailability of a 100 mg dose was 4.7% (90% CI: 3.62 to 6.08) in healthy volunteers
After food intake, nintedanib exposure increased by approximately 20% compared to administration under fasted conditions
The major route of elimination of drug-related radioactivity after oral administration of [ 14 C] nintedanib was via fecal/biliary excretion (93.4% of dose)
clues.substance: Nintedanib is presented as the ethanesulfonate salt (esylate)
clues.safety: The most frequent serious adverse reactions reported in patients treated with OFEV, more than placebo, were bronchitis
The most common adverse events leading to death in patients treated with OFEV, more than placebo, were pneumonia
clues.indication: Treatment of chronic fibrosing interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) with a progressive phenotype
Slowing the rate of decline in pulmonary function in patients with systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD)
clues.mechanism: inhibits multiple receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) and non-receptor tyrosine kinases (nRTKs)
platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR) α and β, fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) 1-3, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) 1-3
involved in the pathogenesis of fibrotic tissue remodeling in ILD
